difficultyReason: Two facts with one obvious confounding variable: museum attendance declined despite renovation, but a competing attraction explains both halves.
stimulus: The Metropolitan Museum's renovated East Wing attracted record foot traffic in its opening month. Yet overall museum attendance fell by 12% in the same period. Visitors had simply shifted from the existing galleries to the new East Wing, with no net increase in total visitors.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Metropolitan Museum is the largest art museum in the Western Hemisphere.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The new East Wing galleries charged admission fees in addition to general museum entry.

choices.label: C
choices.text: During the same period, a major competing museum opened across the street and drew large audiences away from the Metropolitan.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Metropolitan Museum's renovation was completed on schedule and under budget.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The East Wing featured works by contemporary artists that were popular among younger visitors.

explanations.correct: A competing museum opening explains why total attendance fell despite the new East Wing's appeal. The East Wing itself can draw record foot traffic from existing visitors, while the competing museum siphons off visitors who would otherwise have come. Both facts become consistent.
explanations.A: Irrelevant to the discrepancy between the East Wing's success and overall attendance decline.
explanations.B: Additional fees would discourage visitors from the new gallery, but this doesn't reconcile the paradox of renovated-wing success with overall attendance loss.
explanations.D: Project completion is unrelated to the attendance discrepancy.
explanations.E: Popularity with younger visitors explains why the East Wing was successful, but doesn't explain why total museum attendance fell.

difficultyReason: Simple self-selection confound: employees who choose flexible schedules may differ systematically from those who don't. One obvious answer identifies this selection effect.
stimulus: A recent survey found that employees with flexible work schedules report higher job satisfaction than those with fixed schedules. Yet when a tech company mandated flexible schedules for all staff, overall employee satisfaction scores actually declined.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent conflict above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Flexible schedules can reduce collaboration and team cohesion if not implemented thoughtfully.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only highly motivated and engaged employees opt into flexible schedules in the first place.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tech company that mandated flexible schedules also raised employee health insurance costs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Employees with flexible schedules work an average of three hours per week more than those with fixed schedules.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Flexible work schedules have become increasingly popular across the technology industry over the past five years.

explanations.correct: If only highly motivated employees self-select into flexible schedules, their higher satisfaction reflects their motivation, not the schedule itself. Mandating flexibility for unmotivated staff won't boost their satisfaction. This resolves the paradox.
explanations.A: While true, this would deepen the paradox by giving a reason flexible schedules harm satisfaction. We need to explain why voluntary users report higher satisfaction despite this drawback.
explanations.C: A confounding policy change that affects satisfaction, but doesn't explain the original survey finding or resolve the core discrepancy.
explanations.D: Longer hours would reduce satisfaction, making it harder to explain why voluntary users are more satisfied initially.
explanations.E: Industry trends are irrelevant to the discrepancy between voluntary and mandatory adoption outcomes.

difficultyReason: Medical intervention paradox: a successful treatment for one group fails at the population level. Simple confound: the treatment is given to sicker patients.
stimulus: A newly approved antihypertensive drug proved highly effective in clinical trials, reducing blood pressure in 85% of patients who took it. Yet in hospitals across the country, the drug has had no measurable effect on overall patient mortality rates.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The antihypertensive drug can occasionally cause harmful side effects in patients over age 70.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clinical trials for the drug were conducted in a controlled environment with carefully selected participants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In hospitals, the drug is typically prescribed only to the most severely hypertensive patients, whose other comorbidities were the primary cause of death.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The drug works best when combined with lifestyle modifications such as dietary changes and exercise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many competing antihypertensive drugs have been on the market for over a decade.

explanations.correct: In trials, the drug reduced blood pressure (measured outcome). In hospitals, it's given to the sickest patients, whose mortality is driven by other comorbidities, not hypertension alone. Lower blood pressure doesn't prevent death from other causes. This explains the discrepancy.
explanations.A: Side effects would worsen outcomes, deepening the paradox rather than resolving it.
explanations.B: Explains why trials succeeded, but not why hospital outcomes differ—doesn't bridge the paradox.
explanations.D: Lifestyle factors outside the drug's control don't explain the gap between trial efficacy and hospital outcomes.
explanations.E: Competition is irrelevant to the discrepancy between the drug's efficacy and its impact on mortality.

difficultyReason: Economic paradox: price reduction fails to increase sales. Obvious confound: external market shift (e.g., competitor or changed demand).
stimulus: A retailer reduced prices on winter coats by 20% in January to clear inventory. Yet sales of winter coats actually fell by 8% compared to the same month last year.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this unexpected result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: January is typically a slow month for coat sales because much of the winter season has already passed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The retailer's competitors offered summer clothing at discount prices during the same period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An unusually warm January that year reduced consumer demand for winter coats across the entire market.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The retailer's coat inventory consisted of styles that were considered outdated by current fashion standards.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Winter coat manufacturers increased their wholesale prices by 15% earlier that fiscal year.

explanations.correct: Unusually warm weather reduces demand for coats across the market, not just at this retailer. Even with a 20% price cut, fewer people want coats. This explains why the price reduction failed to boost sales.
explanations.A: Irrelevant; January seasonality doesn't explain why prices down but sales down too.
explanations.B: Competitor discounts are a market shift, but summer clothes aren't substitutes for winter coats.
explanations.D: Outdated styles explain slow sales, but not why prices down and sales down—this deepens the paradox.
explanations.E: Wholesale price increases wouldn't cause retail prices to drop or explain the sales decline.

difficultyReason: Simple temporal/compositional shift: reading scores improved overall but appear to fall for a subgroup. Resolution: student population composition changed.
stimulus: State educational data show that test scores in mathematics rose by 6% on average over five years. Yet mathematics teachers report that the students in their classrooms are less prepared and struggle more than students did five years ago.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to reconcile this apparent conflict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The state's standardized mathematics test was redesigned to be slightly easier two years into the five-year period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A significant influx of students from schools with weaker mathematics curricula transferred into the state's public school system during this period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many experienced mathematics teachers retired and were replaced by less experienced teachers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students now spend more time on mathematics homework than they did five years ago.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enrollment in advanced mathematics courses has declined in the state over the past five years.

explanations.correct: If the student population changed (influx of less-prepared students), average state scores could rise due to improved performance by original students, while classroom composition feels weaker. Teachers see a less-prepared cohort within their classrooms even as state averages rise.
explanations.A: Easier test would artificially raise scores, but doesn't explain why teachers see weaker students.
explanations.C: Less experienced teachers would likely lower performance, not raise state averages while students struggle.
explanations.D: More homework might improve performance, but not explain why teachers report students are less prepared.
explanations.E: Lower advanced enrollment doesn't explain the discrepancy between rising averages and weaker students in classrooms.

difficultyReason: Environmental paradox: conservation effort fails at scale. Simple confound: underlying problem worsens or offsetting behavior emerges.
stimulus: A city promoted residential water conservation with rebates for low-flow faucets and toilets. Participating households reduced water use by 18% per household. Yet the city's total water consumption remained unchanged.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low-flow faucets require more frequent use because they deliver less water per minute.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Non-participating households increased their water consumption to offset the conservation gains of their neighbors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The rebate program was more popular in wealthy neighborhoods than in lower-income neighborhoods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Water treatment and delivery infrastructure in the city was upgraded during the same period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The city's population grew by 18% during the conservation program period.

explanations.correct: Population growth of 18% would offset the 18% per-household savings exactly, leaving total consumption flat. Both facts become consistent: households conserve successfully, but the city's total consumption stays the same due to more households overall.
explanations.A: More frequent use would reduce the benefit of low-flow devices, but doesn't explain why total city consumption didn't drop.
explanations.B: Offsetting consumption by non-participants is implausible and poorly motivated.
explanations.D: Infrastructure upgrades don't explain why the conservation gains vanished at the city level.
explanations.C: Unequal program uptake doesn't fully explain zero net change in total consumption.

difficultyReason: Legal/ethical paradox: rule intended to improve fairness produces opposite effect. Resolution: definitional or scope mismatch.
stimulus: A law was enacted to reduce racial disparities in criminal sentencing by limiting judges' discretion. Yet analysis found that sentences remained equally disparate after the law took effect.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this apparent conflict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Judges have been receiving additional training on implicit bias since the law was passed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prosecutors gained greater discretion in charging decisions and began charging defendants from certain racial groups with more serious crimes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The law applied only to crimes that carry a sentence of more than ten years imprisonment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Criminal defense lawyers became more experienced at negotiating plea agreements after the law took effect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The law was widely publicized and was well understood by all members of the judiciary.

explanations.correct: Limiting judicial discretion pushed disparity-creation upstream: prosecutors charged defendants differently by race, producing the same disparities before judges even sentenced. The law reduced judicial discretion but prosecutors filled the gap. Disparities persist.
explanations.A: Bias training would likely reduce disparities, not explain their persistence.
explanations.C: Scope limitation doesn't explain equal disparities in covered versus uncovered crimes.
explanations.D: Better plea negotiations don't explain why disparities persisted after the law.
explanations.E: Public understanding doesn't explain why disparities remained unchanged.

difficultyReason: Technology adoption paradox: efficiency improvement doesn't increase output. Obvious resolution: productivity gains redirected to other uses or quality improvements.
stimulus: A manufacturing plant installed new automated machinery that increased production efficiency by 25%. Yet the plant's total output of finished goods remained the same as before the equipment was installed.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this unexpected outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The automated machinery required substantial retraining of the plant's workforce.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The new machinery was designed to reduce manufacturing defects and improve product quality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The plant had previously operated at maximum capacity given market demand for its products.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maintenance costs for the new equipment were higher than for the old equipment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The new machinery is expected to have a useful lifespan of at least twenty years.

explanations.correct: If the plant was already operating at maximum capacity and market demand hadn't increased, the efficiency gain allows it to maintain output while reducing labor hours or costs—not increase output. Output stays flat because demand, not capacity, was the constraint.
explanations.A: Retraining costs don't explain why output stayed the same despite 25% efficiency gain.
explanations.B: Quality improvement is orthogonal to the discrepancy between efficiency and output quantity.
explanations.D: Higher maintenance costs affect profit, not output quantity.
explanations.E: Equipment lifespan is irrelevant to the output paradox.

difficultyReason: Linguistic/definitional paradox: word frequency rises but usage declines. Resolution: definition or measurement scope shift (e.g., frequency in one corpus but actual speech different).
stimulus: Linguists have found that the word "utilize" appears more frequently in published academic writing today than it did twenty years ago. Yet surveys of academic speakers indicate that fewer scholars actually use the word when speaking in professional settings.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve this apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The word "utilize" is easier to type than to pronounce in a natural-sounding way.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Academic journals have explicitly encouraged authors to use more varied and sophisticated vocabulary in recent years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The word "utilize" was already at a high frequency in academic writing twenty years ago.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spoken academic discourse and written academic prose have diverged, with written work becoming increasingly formal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The word "utilize" is derived from Latin, whereas most common English words are derived from Germanic roots.

explanations.correct: If written prose has become more formal and "utilize" more frequent in writing, but speech has become less formal and "utilize" less frequent in speaking, both observations are consistent. The domains diverged—writing and speech follow different trends.
explanations.A: Typing versus pronunciation ease doesn't explain the frequency difference between writing and speech.
explanations.B: Encouragement to use varied vocabulary doesn't target "utilize" specifically.
explanations.C: High baseline frequency doesn't explain why it rose in writing but fell in speech.
explanations.E: Etymological origin is unrelated to frequency trends or the written-spoken distinction.

difficultyReason: Historical paradox: same action produces different outcomes. Simple resolution: contextual or temporal difference that changes the meaning of the action.
stimulus: In the early twentieth century, many nations extended voting rights to women, expecting this to transform political landscapes dramatically. Yet in most of these nations, electoral outcomes and policy priorities shifted only marginally after women gained the vote.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain this apparent conflict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Women's voting patterns tended to reflect the voting patterns of male family members in their household.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many nations also reformed their tax codes in the early twentieth century.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Women's literacy rates were generally higher in nations that granted voting rights earlier.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The extension of voting rights to women was celebrated by many international observers as a moral victory.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many nations also expanded public education around the same time women gained the vote.

explanations.correct: If women's votes aligned with men's—reflecting household patriarchal influence or shared socioeconomic interests—then women voting wouldn't change electoral outcomes. Adding votes for the same preferences doesn't shift results. Both facts become consistent.
explanations.B: Tax code reforms are orthogonal to the impact of female suffrage on electoral outcomes.
explanations.C: Higher literacy would predict greater political independence, not explain why outcomes stayed stable.
explanations.D: Moral celebration doesn't explain why electoral results remained marginal.
explanations.E: Educational expansion is unrelated to the narrowness of female suffrage's electoral impact.
